transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

I can’t seem to stay focused long enough to get through all the reports and planning tasks my job requires anymore. I was promoted to manage a larger medical service line a couple of years ago and the workload has increased significantly. My primary care doctor actually suggested I get evaluated for possible ADHD because of these persistent focus issues.
Have you struggled with focus, organization, or completing tasks since childhood or your school years, or did these difficulties only start after your promotion?

Honestly, these struggles actually go back to my childhood; back in elementary school, my report cards always said I was smart but "daydreamed" and missed instructions, and my parents had to sit with me for hours to get me through homework. I managed to compensate for a long time, but taking on this larger service line about two years ago made the problems much more severe and harder to hide.
Along with these focus issues, do you frequently experience persistent, hard-to-control worry about everyday things, or have you been feeling down, sad, or hopeless lately?

No, I wouldn't say I have persistent worry about everyday things, and I don't feel hopeless or depressed. I do feel very stressed, frustrated, and tired, but it is specifically tied to my struggles with focus and keeping up at work. It feels more like situational frustration rather than a general sense of anxiety or sadness.
Do you also tend to feel physically restless, fidgety, or find yourself acting or speaking on impulse, both now and when you were younger?

No, I’ve never really struggled with physical restlessness, fidgeting, or impulsivity, either now or as a child. My difficulties have always been much more about internal focus, daydreaming, and my mind drifting away. I've never been physically hyperactive.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong history of inattention, daydreaming, and organizational difficulties dating back to elementary school. These symptoms have persisted into adulthood and have caused significant functional impairment at work following a recent promotion. The patient explicitly denies symptoms of hyperactivity, impulsivity, generalized anxiety, or depressive disorders. This clinical presentation is highly characteristic of Attention Deficit Disorder without hyperactivity, classified under F98.8 in ICD-10.
